Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

papers.title: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching
papers.summary: Individual-level genotype data underpin genetic discovery, disease-risk modeling, and therapeutic development, yet many critical settings remain data-limited, including underrepresented ancestries, rare or imbalanced disease cohorts, and restricted-access biobanks. Conditional synthetic genome generation would support privacy-aware benchmarking, simulation, and data augmentation, but requires learning an ultra-high-dimensional discrete distribution over hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of correlated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), or sites of DNA variation. We introduce HELICS: High-fidelity gEneration via Latent Interpolant Conditional Synthesis, a phasing-free latent flow matching framework for genome-wide SNP-level generation from biobank-scale genotype data. HELICS tokenizes chromosomes with convolutional autoencoders, reducing >600K SNPs to 4,096 continuous latent tokens, and trains a transformer parameterized conditional flow matching model over the concatenated multi-chromosome latent representation. Trained on over 417K genomes in the UK Biobank, HELICS generates genome-wide common-variant synthetic cohorts without haplotype phasing and achieves stronger fidelity to real genotypes than existing haplotype-based simulators, including high allele-frequency agreement in external evaluation and superior preservation of local and long-range SNP correlation structure. Conditioning on ancestry and genetic liability summaries enables targeted generation across genetic risk profiles; in perturbation analyses, by increasing the conditioned disease trait liability, HELICS induces SNP-level dosage changes in generated genomes that are highly correlated with published association weights. HELICS provides a scalable generative modeling framework for SNP-level genome data and a path toward conditional synthetic cohorts for data-limited genetic studies.

papers.title: Many Hands Make Light Work: Long-Term Effect Inference for the Experiment Reservoir
papers.summary: The surrogate index method is the modern standard for estimation of long-term effects in a designed experiment using only short-term outcomes. This method relies on the surrogacy and comparability assumptions which may be violated in practice leading to estimation bias. We propose a new method called Experiment Reservoir Surrogate (ERS) which leverages a reservoir of historical long-term experiments that is common in large-scale experimentation platforms. ERS avoids the surrogacy assumption by predicting the long-term average treatment effect directly, and relaxes the comparability assumption by matching to similar historical experiments, without requiring every experiment in the reservoir to be comparable to the target experiment. Moreover, ERS is memory-efficient, as it only requires aggregate data for each time period, instead of raw individual-level data. We theoretically justify the improved efficiency of ERS and demonstrate the improvement empirically on a reservoir of experiments from the online platform DoorDash.

papers.title: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
papers.summary: Large language models are known to be sycophantic, over-complying with users even when doing so is unproductive. When these models act as coding agents, this can be costly: an agent that keeps editing after no edit improves the code writes churn, technical debt, and review burden into the codebase. Yet the consequences of sycophancy in software engineering remain largely understudied. To understand them, we run a controlled study of iterative refactoring, an open-ended task with no stopping criterion, where any edit an agent makes once the code is already clean reflects compliance rather than improvement. Across algorithmic (n=50) and object-oriented (n=10) suites, we repeatedly ask two widely used agents, Codex and Claude Code, to refactor further across five models. Over 3,000 turns, we define six behavioral signals of over-compliance. We hypothesized that a capable agent would stop once it recognized an optimized codebase; none did. Every model kept editing, rewriting up to 31x the original codebase before first stopping and resuming edits even after declaring the task complete. Over-compliance is a costly, multi-turn behavior that compounds with every turn, and our six signals give developers and tool builders a way to detect and curb it.

papers.title: Enhancing Clinical Classifier Robustness with Deep Representation Learning Based OOD Detection on DNA Methylation Data
papers.summary: DNA methylation (DNAM) array-based tumor classification is a powerful clinical diagnostic tool, but models trained on fixed reference cohorts can produce faulty predictions for tumor types not represented in the training distribution. We propose an end-to-end deep representation learning-based out-of-distribution (OOD) detection framework for DNAm array data. Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers were trained on public sarcoma (SARC) (GSE140686) and brain tumor (BT) (GSE90496) cohorts, and feature vectors were extracted from bottleneck layers. Five OOD methods, including 1dimension (1D)-Subspace Analysis (1D-SSA), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Ridge Regression, Mahalanobis Distance (MD), and Sum of Squared Distances (SSD), were explored with 200 and 500-dimensional embeddings. Spectral discrepancy was used to discriminate in-distribution (IND) from OOD samples. Performance was measured via cross-validation, holdout samples, and an independent clinical dataset. 1D-SSA was the most effective approach. In the sarcoma-IND/brain tumor-OOD setting, the framework achieved an AUROC of 0.975 and True Negative Rate (TNR)@95TPR of 0.930, and an AUROC of 0.9569 and TNR@95TPR of 0.8660 for the brain tumor-IND/sarcoma-OOD setting. On the independent clinical test set, the method yielded a mean AUROC of 0.976, a DE of 0.032, an FPR@95TPR of 0.065, and a TNR@95TPR of 0.935. These results show deep representation-based OOD detection as a practical quality-control layer for clinical-grade methylation-based tumor classification systems.

papers.title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
papers.summary: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.

papers.title: Nuclear Data Evaluation Utilizing Bayesian Monte Carlo Methods
papers.summary: While the body of experimental nuclear data continues to grow at a rapid pace, significant gaps persist. The lack of evaluated experimental data is far more pronounced in charged-particle reactions which are essential to a large portion of the isotope production community for vital medical, industrial, and national security interests. In the absence of experimental and evaluated data, isotope production relies on theoretical models that may result in low yield and isotopic impurities. This work investigates model and parameter adjustments in TALYS 2.0 to establish uncertainty bands on proton-induced cross sections, highlight influential parameters in calculations, and constrain adjustments within physically defensible bounds. The EXFOR dataset for proton-induced reactions on natural copper, comprised of 24 independent cross sections, was used for iterative Bayesian model updating. Upon convergence, parameters and their uncertainties were compared against 23 cumulative cross sections from EXFOR, highlighting the limitations of generalization. Various machine learning models were leveraged to predict TALYS performance, with a small neural network showing useful ranking capabilities across several generations, suggesting the use of a surrogate approach to screening for future evaluations.

papers.title: Event definition and the branching ratio: Hawkes estimates of price-change clustering in the consolidated quote feed
papers.summary: Hawkes models of price changes in the consolidated US quote feed find a sub-millisecond kernel component and a branching ratio near criticality. We show that in large-tick stocks the first is the feed's construction: half of NBBO changes are locks or depleted quotes, resolved within a millisecond, which the model reads as excitation. Defining the event as a mid-price level persisting for one millisecond removes the component. Raw fits put three times the clean kernel mass within one second, which a simulation reproduces. Since the total branching ratio trades off against the baseline, we report kernel mass on a fixed window.
papers.comment: Submitted to the Journal of Financial Econometrics

papers.title: Quark Saturation in Magnetized Pure Neutron Matter
papers.summary: We study how magnetic fields affect the onset of quark saturation, which limits the domain of applicability of a purely baryonic description. We consider matter composed of electrically neutral $ddu$ baryons, including neutron- and $Δ^0$-like states. Using a simple constituent-quark model, we compute the baryon wave functions and spectra in magnetic fields. The magnetic field polarizes the spin-flavor structure, compresses the internal wave function in the transverse direction, and strongly suppresses the transverse kinetic energy. From the baryon wave functions, we construct the one-body reduced density matrix and derive the corresponding single-quark distributions in longitudinal momentum and Landau-level space. We then use these distributions to evaluate quark occupation probabilities in an ideal baryon gas and determine the onset of quark saturation. At finite magnetic field in the $+z$-direction, the $d_\downarrow$ quark in the lowest Landau level reaches saturation first. The resulting saturation density depends nonmonotonically on the magnetic-field strength: it decreases at weak fields and increases at stronger fields. This behavior reflects the competition between spin-flavor polarization, which promotes saturation, and transverse spatial squeezing, which delays saturation by broadening of the quark transverse momentum distribution.
papers.comment: 31 pages, 9 figures; a contribution to the special issue "Magnetized Dense Matter in Compact Stars: From Fundamental Properties to Astrophysical Observables"

papers.title: Measurement of antideuteron and net-$Λ$ number fluctuations at the Large Hadron Collider
papers.summary: The recent measurements of event-by-event correlations between the antideuteron and antiproton numbers in Pb$-$Pb collisions at the LHC deviate from the statistical hadronization model parameterizations that describe the yields and fluctuations of light-flavored hadrons. This discrepancy may stem from nucleosynthesis processes involved in the formation of composite states like antideuterons. In this letter, we present the first measurement of the antideuteron$-$net-$Λ$ number correlation obtained in Pb$-$Pb collisions with the ALICE detector. This quantity is mostly sensitive to the quantum-number correlations induced by the hadronization process, as $Λ$ hyperons are not constituents of antideuterons. Both the antideuteron$-$net-$Λ$ number correlation and the normalized second-order cumulant of the net-$Λ$ number are well described by the statistical hadronization model implemented in Thermal-FIST. This establishes strong evidence that the antideuteron$-$antiproton correlation is driven by the nucleosynthesis processes, while the correlation between antideuterons and non-nucleonic hadrons is primarily sensitive to the hadronization mechanism.
papers.comment: 20 pages, 2 captioned figures, authors from page 15, submitted to PRL, figures at http://alice-publications.web.cern.ch/node/13689

papers.title: Chebyshev-expanded covariant density functional from relativistic Brueckner theory
papers.summary: We construct a density-dependent covariant energy density functional (CE-ME1) from full-Dirac-space relativistic Brueckner--Hartree--Fock (RBHF) self-energies and the corresponding equation of state. The space-like component $U_V$ is incorporated at the Fermi surface through reduced scalar and time-like self-energies, which are mapped onto local Hartree $σ$, $ω$, $δ$, and $ρ$ channels. The density-dependent couplings are represented by cubic Chebyshev polynomials over the density range $0.08\leqρ\leq0.48~{\rm fm}^{-3}$. A constrained thermodynamic calibration uses 199 RBHF energy-per-particle values from published microscopic computations at six isospin asymmetries, while maintaining positive, monotonic couplings. The Bonn-A RBHF saturation point, incompressibility $K_\infty=258$ MeV, symmetry energy $J=33.1$ MeV, and slope $L=65.2$ MeV are reproduced. The predicted curvature $K_{\rm sym}=33$ MeV differs from the published RBHF value of $-67$ MeV, illustrating the derivative sensitivity of the local reduction. The combined energy RMS is $0.613$ MeV, measuring model discrepancy rather than statistical uncertainty. Uniform matter remains mechanically stable and causal above saturation within the calibrated range. In cold charge-neutral $npeμ$ matter, CE-ME1 reasonably reproduces the interpolated RBHF pressure and proton fraction over most of the interval, although the pressure discrepancy increases near its upper edge. The DD-ME2 benchmark is stiffer and predicts a lower proton fraction at high density.

papers.title: Subpercent accuracy in molecular electric quadrupole coupling: nuclear-size and relativistic effects in RaF
papers.summary: We report a benchmark study of the electric-quadrupole hyperfine interaction in the electronic ground state of the RaF molecule, including finite-nuclear-size effects. The calculations include relativistic effects using the Dirac-Coulomb-Breit Hamiltonian and electron correlation up to perturbative quadruple excitations within the coupled cluster framework. At the achieved level of accuracy, penetration of the electronic density into the finite nuclear quadrupole distribution produces a non-negligible correction to the usual electric field gradient (EFG) description at the center of the nucleus and must be considered. At a fixed rms charge radius, the EFG is much less sensitive to the shape of the monopole nuclear charge distribution: electron wavefunctions computed using the Gaussian and Fermi nuclear charge models yield nearly identical EFGs. The recommended effective EFG parameter for the $X\,{}^{2}Σ_{1/2}$ electronic ground state is $\langle q\rangle_0=-5.178(21)$ a.u., with an estimated uncertainty reduced by an order of magnitude compared to previous studies. Combined with future measurements of electric-quadrupole hyperfine coupling constants in RaF, this result can be used to determine the nuclear quadrupole moments of Ra isotopes with record precision.

papers.title: Does Ecosystem Activity Validate TVL?
papers.summary: Total value locked (TVL) is widely used to assess decentralized finance ecosystems. Prior evidence finds that portfolios formed on TVL alone are spanned by the crypto market portfolio (Brigida 2025). This paper asks whether TVL becomes more informative when combined with measures of adoption, usage, development, protocol revenue, or social attention. I construct weekly value-weighted 2x3 portfolios that independently sort tokens on TVL-to-market-cap and one of seven ecosystem-activity ratios. Portfolio returns are computed from token prices using lagged-market-capitalization weights and evaluated against crypto market and size factors. Across the available 2022-2025 samples, none of the six on-chain double sorts rejects the benchmark after controlling for multiple testing. The same conclusion holds over 83 common weeks for which social-attention data are available. Several specifications reject at unadjusted levels, but none survives Holm adjustment. The social-attention rejection is only marginal under asymptotic inference and is insignificant under a moving-block bootstrap. Equal-weighted portfolios and formal parameter-stability tests lead to the same broad conclusion. The evidence therefore does not show that ecosystem activity reliably transforms TVL into an incremental return signal.

papers.title: Temporal smoothness constraints on efficient neurobiological codes imply temporal specialization
papers.summary: Neurobiological circuits may be energy efficient in part because there is a division of labor: different subsystems compute or represent different things. In light of this, it is interesting that a major difference between subsystems is the time scale on which they typically vary. Here, we argue that temporal smoothness constraints---the idea that it may be energetically costly for systems to vary much more quickly than their typical time scale---imply a certain division of labor with respect to temporal stimulus features. In particular, slow subsystems ought to represent slowly varying stimulus features, and fast subsystems ought to represent quickly varying features. We formulate a novel efficient coding model that we use to investigate this claim, and exactly solve for the optimal division of labor. In addition to finding that slower subsystems ought to represent more slowly varying temporal features, we find surprising structure of mathematical interest: optimal codes have subsystems which represent orthogonal temporal features, and which correspond to the eigenfunctions of a Sturm-Liouville problem.

papers.title: Optimally Selling Heterogeneous Objects by Quantity
papers.summary: I study the optimality of selling K heterogeneous objects to a buyer with private values through a quantity menu: the seller posts a price for each number of objects, and the buyer chooses a quantity, pays its price, and selects any objects up to that quantity. I propose a pricing method that aggregates critical values for second differences of quantity values (the highest values attainable at each quantity). Critical values can be determined separately when each second difference's conditional inverse-hazard ratio depends only on that difference. For additive values, I show that the resulting menu is optimal among all incentive-compatible and individually rational mechanisms under explicit distributional and support conditions, including ex ante symmetry across object labels. A separate result applies the same pricing method to obtain an optimal menu for nonadditive bundle values without ex ante symmetry, assuming free disposal, independence between the quantity-value vector and the vector of bundle shortfalls from their respective quantity values, and corresponding distributional and support conditions. For an arbitrary number of objects, applications yield explicit optimal menus that involve quantity discounts, sparse quantity options, or two-part tariffs. These results differ from those establishing the optimality of pure bundling in Haghpanah and Hartline (2021), nested bundling in Yang (2025), separate sales in Kwak (2026), and core-peripheral bundling in Zhong (2026).

papers.title: Evidence of partonic collectivity in OO collisions through the measurement of $φ$, K$^0_{\rm S}$, and $Λ$ elliptic flow
papers.summary: The first measurement of the elliptic-flow coefficient ($v_{2}$) of $φ$, K$^0_{\rm S}$, and $Λ(\overlineΛ)$ hadrons performed in OO collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=5.36$ TeV with the ALICE detector is presented as a function of transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) in central and semi-central collisions. For the $φ$ meson, in particular, this is the first measurement of the elliptic flow in a small collision system. At low $p_{\rm T}$, a characteristic mass ordering of $v_{2}$ is observed, consistent with collective expansion of the system, in which heavier hadrons are shifted to higher $p_{\rm T}$ by a common velocity field. At intermediate $p_{\rm T}$, above 3 GeV/$c$, a baryon$-$meson splitting with a $10σ$ significance emerges, with the $Λ(\overlineΛ)$ baryon exhibiting larger $v_{2}$ values than mesons, while, despite its mass being close to the mass of the $Λ$, the $φ$ follows the K$^{0}_{\rm S}$. The $φ$ meson behavior disfavors a purely mass-driven interpretation of the observed patterns and supports the role of hadronization via quark recombination from a collectively flowing partonic medium. These results provide complementary evidence that key signatures of partonic collectivity observed in Pb$-$Pb collisions persist in light nucleus$-$nucleus systems.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 3 captioned figures, 1 table, authors from page 17, submitted to PRL, figures at http://alice-publications.web.cern.ch/node/13688

papers.title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.summary: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

papers.title: Beta decay of potassium-54 reveals the role of two-body currents in neutron-rich nuclei
papers.summary: The beta decay of neutron-rich nuclei probes the microscopic nature of weak interactions in the nuclear medium under extreme conditions. Such weak decays drive the synthesis of heavy elements in astrophysical environments, but remain poorly understood. Far from stability, experimental data are scarce, placing strong demands on ab initio nuclear theory. Two-body weak currents have been proposed as the dominant mechanism responsible for the universal quenching of theoretically predicted Gamow-Teller decay strength. However, direct experimental validation in neutron-rich nuclei has been lacking. Here we measure the beta decay of 54K, a nucleus at the experimental frontier of radioactive ion-beam facilities. In this work, the doubly magic nature of the daughter nucleus 54Ca results in a remarkably simple decay pattern, dominated by a single transition to a neutron-unbound state at 6.2 MeV with a comparative partial half-life logft=4.4(1) or Gamow-Teller decay strength B(GT)=0.26 (+0.08) (-0.04). Our measurement is reproduced by new state-of-the-art calculations of the decay, providing direct evidence for the essential role of two-body currents in nuclear beta decay for systems with a significant neutron excess. We establish a key benchmark for theoretical predictions of weak processes in exotic nuclei.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in Nature Communications

papers.title: Indirect inference in incomplete and partially identified econometric models
papers.summary: We extend the indirect inference principle to structural econometric models that are incomplete, in the sense that a single value of the structural parameter may be compatible with multiple distributions of the observed endogenous variables, so that the structural parameter is typically only partially identified. We define the binding function as the smallest norm of the auxiliary estimating equations over the set of data generating processes compatible with the structural model. Hence, we obtain a confidence region by inverting a test of the hypothesis that the binding function vanishes at the pseudo-true value. A dual characterization based on random set theory makes the binding function computationally tractable. We define the auxiliary model conditionally on the covariates to remove its dependence on the unknown covariate distribution and we show that the binding function is Lipschitz and Hadamard directionally differentiable, so that the numerical delta method delivers valid critical values. We show that the method provides significant computational advantages without relinquishing informativeness in a simulation experiment based on an entry game with 100 potential entrants.

papers.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
papers.summary: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making treatment-effect estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and borrow information across related observations, but existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis generally combine outcome modeling and counterfactual imputation in estimator-specific formulations that can require bespoke sampling algorithms. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency of counterfactual imputation, characterize how pooling affects imputation risk, and develop fast cross-validation for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. Our results show that probabilistic modeling can improve counterfactual imputation, particularly when observation noise is substantial and the pooling structure is informative.

papers.title: From Tariff Changes to Trade Effects: A Practical Framework for Empirical Trade Policy Analysis
papers.summary: After decades of trade liberalization, the 2020s mark a profound shift in the globalization narrative, with tariffs once again becoming a central instrument of trade policy. This reversal also challenges how the effects of trade policy are evaluated. Much of the empirical literature has been developed to assess bilateral tariff reductions or elimination and the associated erosion of preferential advantages. Rising multilateral tariffs pose a different question: they alter not only the trade costs faced by directly affected exporters but also the relative market access of all competing suppliers, potentially reinforcing existing preferences. This paper develops a practical framework for translating tariff changes into trade effects in this new policy environment. We argue that liberalization and protectionism should not be treated as symmetric policy experiments: their effects operate through different changes in relative market access and therefore require careful consideration of how tariff shocks are measured and incorporated into empirical trade models and counterfactual evaluations.

papers.title: MtReNIRS: A Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Transferable Neurovascular Representations
papers.summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a promising approach for monitoring the hemodynamic correlates of neural activity in naturalistic settings. However, existing modeling methods for fNIRS are largely confined to small-scale, single-session data with low sampling rates, driven by high heterogeneity in acquisition devices and optode montages. In addition, the complex spatiotemporal structure of fNIRS signals further restricts model scalability and transferability across settings. As a result, it remains unclear whether a single fNIRS encoder can learn representations that are usable across subjects, tasks, devices, and montages. Here, we show that a montage-aware masked autoencoder, pretrained on 12 public fNIRS datasets spanning 268 subjects and 567 recording hours, learns generalizable neurovascular representations that transfer across three external datasets. Our fNIRS foundation model, MtReNIRS, jointly encodes the slow hemodynamic nature of fNIRS, chromophore identity and cortical location by mapping heterogeneous montages onto a shared anatomical reference. MtReNIRS achieves cross-subject performance on par or better than fully supervised baselines and excels in few-shot within-subject calibration, where it outperforms prior state-of-the-art fNIRS models, while remaining robust to sparse montages. Our results indicate that montage-aware self-supervision yields physiologically grounded, transferable fNIRS representations, providing a scalable foundation for label-efficient brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: Degrading the Grade: Grading Variance as Evidence of Shirking
papers.summary: Variation in grading standards across instructors who teach the same students is evidence of a moral hazard problem, whether or not grades are inflated. The optimal standard is the same for every section of a course, yet grades vary widely across sections. We present a principal-agent model in which instructors who know the optimal standard still depart from it, leniently or harshly, depending on their incentives. Penalizing deviations from the department average leaves the average unchanged but compresses grading variance, which raises student welfare. Disclosing the same information to students instead increases grading variance.

papers.title: Testing strong exogeneity in proxy SVARs with internal synthetic proxies
papers.summary: Proxy SVARs often rely on a single credible proxy, leaving proxy exogeneity untestable. Narrative arguments used to justify proxy validity imply a stronger form of exogeneity. We formalize the strong exogeneity assumption and propose a corresponding test based on internal synthetic proxies. The approach uses the external proxy to locate the target-shock direction in the reduced-form innovations and synthesize the candidate shock into an additional internal synthetic proxies, which allows to test the joint exogeneity of the original and internal synthetic proxy. We derive the large-sample theory for the ISP test and show that the identification strength is governed by a direct measure of the target shock's non-Gaussianity. We study weak identification under asymptotic Gaussianity and develop an identification-robust version of the test. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate the favorable power of the test when the proxy has a low signal-to-noise ratio. Applications to monetary policy and oil supply news shocks find no evidence against the exogeneity of the benchmark proxies.

papers.title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
papers.summary: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

papers.title: Direct measurement of the ${}^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p, γ){}^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ reaction using the DRAGON recoil separator and a hybrid array of $γ$-ray detectors
papers.summary: Background: The $^{23}$Mg$(p,γ)^{24}$Al reaction plays a key role in nova nucleosynthesis, serving as a bridge between the Ne-Na and Mg-Al cycles and impacting synthesis of a wide variety of nuclides. It is crucial that the rate of this reaction be well constrained by experimental data, in particular the properties of the key resonance at $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV, which dominates the rate at nova temperatures. Purpose: Our study aims to improve experimental constraints on the energy and strength of the key $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV $^{23}$Mg$(p,γ)^{24}$Al resonance through a new direct measurement of its strength and energy. Methods: We used a $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}$ radioactive beam to directly observe capture into the $E_{\mathrm{cm}}\approx480$ keV resonance in inverse kinematics. The $^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ recoils were selected by the DRAGON recoil separator, and coincident $γ$ rays were measured in a hybrid $\mathrm{LaBr}_3/\mathrm{CeBr}_3/\mathrm{BGO}$ scintillator array. The $^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ singles yield was used to determine the resonance strength, while the time difference between the coincident $γ$ rays and the incident beam was used to determine the resonance energy. Results: We obtained a strength of $ωγ=38(7)$ meV and an energy of $E_{\mathrm{cm}}=478.8(26)$ keV for the key astrophysical $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p,γ)^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ resonance. Conclusions: Our reported strength is in excellent agreement with the previously reported direct measurement, as well as shell model calculations. Our energy is in good agreement with earlier indirect measurements. Reaction rate calculations incorporating our results indicate that the $^{23}\mathrm{Mg}(p,γ)^{24}\mathrm{Al}$ rate is constrained to a $1σ$ up/down factor of 1.5 or smaller in the nova temperature range of 0.2--0.4 GK.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables, 1 supplemental material, accepted for publication in Phys Rev C

papers.title: On the stability of learning
papers.summary: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true---learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

papers.title: Adequacy radii for stepped-wedge trials with time-varying effects
papers.summary: Complete stepped-wedge designs guarantee eventual intervention delivery, but their final periods contain no concurrent controls. Under exposure-time heterogeneity this creates a design-analysis tension: a constant-effect analysis can be precise while targeting a design-dependent contrast, whereas an exposure-time indicator (ETI) analysis targets a prespecified time-averaged effect but may be much less precise. We develop an adequacy radius that quantifies the size of exposure-time heterogeneity compatible with a prespecified tolerance for estimand mismatch, and combine it with precision calculations to compare complete wedges with rollout-constrained hybrid designs that retain a wait-list arm. For a balanced wedge with a wait-list under the Hussey-Hughes model, the wait-list share and the correlation act on the constant-effect GLS estimand through a single scalar; we prove that the radius increases strictly with the wait-list share and decreases strictly with the within-cluster correlation, but remains bounded. Numerical optimisation and a model-based redesign of a weekend allied-health trial show that intermediate hybrids make estimand-aligned ETI analysis materially more affordable, giving a robustness-precision frontier rather than a binary choice between a complete wedge and a parallel trial. A second trial, of digital adherence support for tuberculosis treatment, has the same radius but no detectable heterogeneity; its test of a constant effect would detect heterogeneity large enough to halve the coverage of the nominal interval only 37% of the time. The contribution is a diagnostic and design principle: when exposure-time heterogeneity is plausible, retaining concurrent controls reduces the price of analysing the estimand one intends to report.

papers.title: Dynamic heart rate variability for classification of arrhythmia burden
papers.summary: Purpose: Heart rate variability (HRV) may provide information beyond heart rate (HR) for identifying arrhythmia burden, but the value of temporal HRV variation remains unclear. This study developed a dynamic HRV measure quantifying the interquartile range of window-level root mean square of successive RR-interval differences (IQRRMSSD) and evaluated its utility in classifying total abnormal-beat and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden compared with the conventional RR-based HRV measure, RMSSD. Methods: Manually annotated 30-minute ECG recordings from 43 individuals were analyzed using overlapping windows. A linear support vector classifier was used to classify individuals as having high or low arrhythmia burden, defined using 1% and 10% burden thresholds. Four feature sets were evaluated: HR alone, HR with RMSSD, HR with IQRRMSSD, and all three measures. Performance was assessed using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Results: HRV-containing feature sets generally outperformed HR alone, depending on outcome and threshold. At the 1% threshold, IQRRMSSD showed particularly high sensitivity for total abnormal-beat and PVC burden ($0.970 \pm 0.064$ and $0.882 \pm 0.193$, respectively). At the 10% threshold, conventional RMSSD showed the strongest overall discrimination, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.947 for PVC burden. Combined features sometimes improved the sensitivity-specificity balance but not overall discrimination. Conclusion: These findings suggest that a conventional RR-based HRV measure is informative for elevated ectopic burden, while a dynamic HRV measure may provide complementary information for lower-burden abnormalities.

papers.title: A theory of noisy linear recurrent neural network learning dynamics
papers.summary: Biological neural networks are noisy: their dynamics involve difficult-to-predict fluctuations which are likely due not just to chaos, but also to a variety of low-level biophysical processes. Despite the omnipresence of intrinsic noise, its theoretical consequences are incompletely understood, especially in the context of learning. For example, does noise meaningfully shape representation learning, or is it better viewed as a nuisance factor whose presence or absence changes little about what solution is found and when? Here, we argue that intrinsic noise can significantly modulate representation learning in recurrent neural networks (RNNs), since it can strongly break solution-space degeneracies and in some cases control whether a non-degenerate solution exists at all. We show that this is true for an analytically tractable model of noisy RNN learning with a linear activation function and white noise inputs. We find that, in the so-called rich regime (where weights are initialized with small values), noise strongly modulates the directions in which the read-in, readout, and recurrent weights align. Moreover, we find that noise produces a kind of phase transition: for sufficiently high noise, a non-degenerate solution is not even optimal if parameter scales are limited (e.g., via regularization). These results extend recent analytic work on RNN representation learning and show that noise can act as a fundamental determinant of representations.

papers.title: Immersive Commons: Designing Ephemeral Spatial Dialogue for Co-Located Mixed Reality Environments
papers.summary: Head-mounted mixed reality (MR) often prioritises individual immersion, potentially drawing attention away from others sharing the room. This paper asks how MR can support co-located spatial dialogue through embodied interaction and activity visible to non-headset observers. We introduce Immersive Commons, a design framework, and Atmos Messages, a prototype combining gesture-based, ephemeral spatial messages with voice transcription, preset text, and a public floor-plan overview. Following a Research through Design approach, fifteen participants created 236 messages across two sessions, including 48 voice-authored messages. Questionnaire responses highlighted playfulness and social awareness, while observations suggested opportunities for exchange grounded in the architectural setting. Interaction clustered near the public display, although this was also where participants put on their headsets. These findings suggest the potential of ephemeral spatial messaging to support co-located exchange, with playfulness, shared visibility, and architectural context informing the design of more social and situated MR experiences.
papers.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at SIGraDi 2026, the Conference of the Iberoamerican Society of Digital Graphics

papers.title: The Evolution and 'Chineseness' of Urban Screens in China: From Propaganda Posters to Smart City Interfaces
papers.summary: Urban screens have become a global feature of the media city, yet their developmental paths are not universal. This paper argues that the evolution of urban screens in China constitutes a distinct paradigm of media urbanism, termed Chineseness, understood here not as cultural essence but as a relational, historically situated configuration of three linked elements: deep-rooted lineages of public communication; state-steered technological leapfrogging driven by industrial policy and mega-events; and a regulatory paradox that enables spectacular scale while tightening operational control. Drawing on a five-stage genealogy (1990-present), a chronology of representative screens, and five paradigmatic cases, the study shows how this configuration produces temporal-spatial compression, the coexistence of multiple technological generations, and privileges collective witnessing over device-centric interactivity. The paper contributes a documented genealogy of Chinese urban screens, develops temporal-spatial compression and collective witnessing as analytical tools for non-Western media ecologies, and positions Chineseness as a globally relevant alternative to market-led models of media architecture.
papers.comment: 14 pages. Accepted at the Media Architecture Biennale 2025 (MAB25), Bangkok

papers.title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
papers.summary: Visual search is ubiquitous in daily life, from locating keys in a messy apartment to finding a tool in a cluttered workshop or an application icon on a desktop screen. While visual attention is to a large extent driven by image content, research in psychology indicates that user cognitive states have a significant influence on attention allocation. A promising way to access information about cognitive states is via Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. Despite this potential, previous works in computational attention modeling have largely disregarded EEG, and related studies in psychology operate with abstract, simplistic stimuli, or even artificially guided search procedures. We bridge this gap with two contributions. First, we present EEGaze 140, the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of free visual search with realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye tracking recordings from 36 participants across 140 naturalistic scenes, covering two scenarios: searching for desktop icons and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. Second, we introduce EEGazeNet, the first method for human attention prediction in visual search that integrates EEG signals. Our approach consists of a EEG guided refinement stage that adapts the output of a state of the art saliency prediction method to the user current cognitive state. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze 140, we show that EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions.

papers.title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
papers.summary: The gap between AI capability deployment and safety assurance is structural and cannot be closed through internal evaluations alone. Analyzing documented harms (2017-2026) across the human lifespan reveals that disparate incidents --- from voice assistants endangering children to AI companions implicated in adolescent suicide and automated care denials for the elderly --- reflect a single failure: evaluating systems against an implicit adult user model. We introduce five developmental moderators structured into a Lifespan Vulnerability Matrix across six life stages. The matrix reveals a nonmonotonic risk distribution: vulnerability peaks at both ends of the lifespan, governance coverage is asymmetrical, and authority to convert model errors into real-world impact is scrutinized least. We then propose a set of lifespan design principles generalizing existing child-protective instruments, and an institution-agnostic, three-tier external evaluation framework --- comprising automated simulation, expert red teaming, and post-deployment monitoring --- indexed directly to matrix risk cells.

papers.title: Reflective Computing
papers.summary: Interactive technology is increasingly built for speed, and generative AI now answers before a question is fully formed. Yet the capacity to pause, interpret and decide for oneself is central to wellbeing, learning and meaningful use. HCI has named paradigms for sensing emotion, changing behavior, calming attention and tracking the self. However, none of them takes human reflection, and the slowing down it requires, as its organizing aim. This article defines that paradigm, reflective computing, and derives it from what thirty years of designs lack. We analyzed 134 interactive systems from 17 ACM venues (1996-2026) in two phases. First, an abductive gap analysis read every system against reflection theory, and seven recurring gaps defined seven dimensions, namely tempo agency, invitational form, interpretive openness, reflective depth, temporal span, protected idleness and ethical non-extraction. Second, two independent coders scored every system with a codebook (Krippendorff's alpha 0.67 to 0.84 for five dimensions; ICC 0.82 for the overall score). The system sets the pace in 51 designs, 74 support only momentary use, only 12 scaffold reflection beyond description, and 56 papers are silent on the inner states they collect. No system expresses all seven dimensions strongly, and only 20 meet the definition. Slow and experience centered design comes closest, whereas persuasive technology and human-AI interaction score lowest. Factor and latent class analyses reveal two cultures of reflection, one working through form and the other through scaffolded thought, which only one system combines. Systems that let people set the pace score markedly higher, even with paradigm and form controlled (odds ratio 13.5). Hence, reflective computing is proposed as a paradigm whose aim is a human capacity rather than a system function, and which treats slowness as valuable only when people choose it.

papers.title: GNN-VIEW: Visual Inspection and Explanation of Graph-based Earth-System Models
papers.summary: Machine learning Earth-system models are becoming increasingly important, and so is their development. Graph-based models, one of the most prominent approaches, allow developers to constrain the learning process before training via graph connectivity. Yet, developing these models remains challenging: the graph is built algorithmically with little intuition about the final result beyond static plotting, which requires extra work and is often not detailed enough. Even after successful training, how the model arrives at forecasts remains obscure. We present GNN-VIEW, an interactive browser-based tool that supports the development of such systems. GNN-VIEW exposes the graph's information pathways, allowing model developers to debug the graph structure before training. After training, GNN-VIEW uses attribution-based explainability to reveal which input features are used by the trained model for a given forecast. This helps developers understand why a model fails. We showcase the usefulness of GNN-VIEW in the construction stage of a graph for an ocean forecasting model, and in explaining poorly predicted precipitation of a trained weather forecasting model during Hurricane Laura.
papers.comment: Accepted to The 2nd Workshop on Advances in Representation Learning for Earth Observation at NeurIPS 2026

papers.title: Phase response approach to networked neural activity models with delays
papers.summary: Networks of delay-coupled neural mass models alternate between synchrony and anti-phase locking as the delay between brain regions increases. The origin of these delay-dependent bands has remained unclear. Here, we show that a single function, the phase interaction function $H$ of an isolated node, predicts where the bands occur and explains why they repeat. For a Wilson--Cowan model with intra-nodal delay $τ$ and inter-nodal delay $ρ$, we compute the limit cycle and phase response, and hence $H$, by harmonic balance. Each band boundary is a zero of $H'$ shifted by the phase lag $Ωρ$, so the bands repeat in $ρ$ with the oscillation period. Simulations of the full delay-differential networks confirm these predictions, from two nodes, where predicted frequencies agree to second order in the coupling strength, to rings, where the theory also identifies coexisting stable twisted states that random initial conditions rarely reach. At weak coupling, the delays at which synchrony gains or loses stability are set by the node dynamics alone, whereas stable anti-phase states require a bipartite network. For a macaque connectome, metastability peaks at the edges of the synchrony bands, where the stability margin of phase-locking vanishes. The reduction is accurate for coupling strengths well below the slowest Floquet exponent of the node, beyond which a phase--amplitude description is needed. More broadly, vanishing phase-locking stability provides a simple route to metastability in delay-coupled oscillator networks and a candidate mechanism for the flexible coordination of brain dynamics.

papers.title: Offline Language-Based Support System for Tactical Decision-Making in Air Combat Operations
papers.summary: An offline language-based support tool is presented to assist pilot training and tactical decision-making in air combat operations. The system, named MATE (Mission Assistant for Training and Evaluation), applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer natural language questions using content extracted from doctrinal and tactical manuals. Built entirely with open-source components, it performs text preprocessing, embedding generation, semantic search, and language generation locally, ensuring full offline functionality. The tool was evaluated by three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots, who rated the answers produced with three open-weight language models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Mistral NeMo 12B) to five tactical questions derived from a publicly available air combat manual. Average ratings ranged from 4.00 to 4.40 on a five-point scale, with Mistral NeMo 12B obtaining the highest score, and the pilots rated the response time of the tool as fully adequate compared to manual search. The relevance of the retrieved content was identified as the main point for improvement. Potential applications are discussed in onboard mission systems, flight simulators, and training environments.
papers.comment: Accepted at the LatinX in AI Workshop @ NeurIPS 2025. 7 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables

papers.title: Revisiting Direct Control: A Field Evaluation of Sensor Fusion Efficacy in Teleoperating Full-Scale Autonomous Vehicles via Bird's Eye View
papers.summary: In autonomous driving, robot teleoperation serves as a critical safety fallback mechanism, requiring operators to assume direct control in the event of system failure. While recent research has pivoted toward high-level supervisory control or simulation-based studies, these approaches often fail to capture the physical dynamics and sensory demands of driving a full-scale vehicle. To address this gap, we evaluated the impact of spatial data representation on operator performance using a real car-sized vehicle in a field experiment with $N = 18$ participants. We compared three visualization interfaces: (i) a standard camera feed baseline, with two bird's-eye views (BEV) from (ii) a raw LiDAR point cloud, and (iii) a sensor fusion of LiDAR and camera data streams. Contrary to prior passive observation studies suggesting that sensor-fusion BEV may hinder awareness, our active-control results demonstrate that such representation significantly outperforms the standard LiDAR BEV in perceived usability ($p \leq 0.0001$) and cognitive task load ($p = 0.01$, NASA-TLX score: 34.58/100) while also being significantly better than the Camera-only view ($p = 0.043$). The fused interface also led to statistically significant reductions in task completion time ($p = 0.0461$) and superior usability (SUS: 77.9/100) compared to those of the Camera-only and LiDAR-only views. By synthesizing objective performance data with comprehensive subjective assessments, we demonstrate that BEV fusion maximizes safety margins while minimizing the operator's mental demand. These findings challenge existing teleoperation conventions and provide an empirically validated approach for designing robust remote piloting systems.
papers.comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)

papers.title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
papers.summary: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

papers.title: Multiscale MIGHT: Modeling Local and Systemic Particle Transport in the Cardiovascular System
papers.summary: Analytical models of signaling molecule (SM) transport in the cardiovascular system (CVS) force a choice between whole-body scope and vessel-level resolution: Pharmacokinetic models for systemic transport lump each organ and lack small-scale structure, whereas synthetic molecular communication (MC) channel models resolve branched vessel networks (VNs) only for a single pass or capture recirculation only in topologically simple loops, and only partially include SM degradation. To close this gap, we propose Multiscale MIGHT, an extension of the Mixture of Inverse Gaussians for Hemodynamic Transport (MIGHT) model that jointly captures branched topologies, closed-loop circulation, organ clearance, and chemical degradation of SMs. First, we connect the ends of a branched VN to form a closed loop with local and global SM degradation, model the closed-loop channel impulse response for arbitrary transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) positions as a Laplace-domain feedback system, and approximate it in closed form by an inverse Gaussian mixture over multi-pass trajectories. The model is validated against finite-element simulations in COMSOL. Second, we set up a whole-body model, where an exemplary local VN, resolved at vessel-level detail, is embedded into the remaining systemic circulation, represented by lumped organ blocks. We simulate whole-body SM transport for various Tx sites and SM species. Our results show that, at an Rx in a local VN, only the initial pass produces a distinct peak in the SM concentration, significantly shaped by the local vasculature in case of small Tx-Rx distances; subsequent passes arrive strongly dispersed and are shaped almost entirely by organ clearance and chemical degradation rather than by the local VN topology.
papers.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures; Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027

papers.title: High-resolution tactile observation makes hidden racket-control mechanisms learnable
papers.summary: Experts can master fine hand-object manipulation skills, yet limited conscious perception of rapid tactile interactions hinders their ability to articulate the underlying control mechanisms. Badminton racket control requires rapid, fine hand-force coordination, providing a demanding testbed for uncovering these mechanisms. An 864-node tactile-inertial glove with synchronized 100-Hz acquisition recorded over 14,000 strokes from more than 70 participants across five skills. Inspired by sensorimotor control, our mechanics-grounded two-layer framework inferred object-driving and grip-stabilizing control from tactile history, while resolving their spatiotemporal force realization. We found that higher proficiency was associated with selective rather than extensive control: greater skill specificity, anticipatory regulation, focal distal modulation and lower geometric torque cancellation, while spatiotemporal coordination showed a non-monotonic acquire-refine pattern. We translated these mechanisms into personalized guidance targeting force control and force-motion coordination. In a randomized cohort, mechanism-guided learners gained 0.72 expert-rated skill levels versus 0.05 with level-only feedback, making control mechanisms actionable.
papers.comment: 58 pages, including 14 pages of main text and 44 pages of supplementary information. 5 main figures and 19 supplementary figures

papers.title: Beyond Being Accurate: Implications for Using Natural Language Descriptions for Accessible 3D Modeling with~Blind and Low Vision Makers
papers.summary: People who are blind or have low vision (BLV) are largely excluded from 3D modeling tools that rely on visual representations of geometry. Natural language descriptions offer a potential path to accessibility, but it is unclear whether language alone can support the deep spatial understanding that editing, not just browsing, requires. Advances in generative AI offer the promise of automatic model description, yet descriptions suited to BLV modelers are structurally distinct from alt-text and from existing 3D model captioning datasets, and the domain-specific requirements for generating them are not well understood. We address this through two coordinated studies: an autoethnographic pilot in which the blind first author worked with 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies, and a Wizard-of-Oz main study that applied those strategies as idealized scripts with 10 BLV participants. We identify a systematic use-to-editing gap: descriptions that support accurate but incomplete mental models are insufficient for specifying modifications, because editing requires knowing the state of features the user did not know to ask about. We show that this gap produces four failure types (accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation) that accuracy-focused evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We propose a two-phase evaluation framework that diagnoses the failure type a description system exhibits and guides developers toward targeted design interventions, thereby providing a methodological standard for assessing whether description-based systems genuinely support BLV modelers as creators.

papers.title: Negative-Power Density of States in Chiral-Orthogonal Disordered Systems and the IR Phase of QCD
papers.summary: The recently discovered IR phase of QCD is characterized by an infrared (IR) sector of Dirac modes that separates and dynamically decouples from the bulk of the spectrum, becoming scale invariant in the process [1]. Among key features of this IR sector is the negative power-law behavior of Dirac spectral density near zero with power $p$ close to $-1$. Here we start investigating to what extent can this behavior be mimicked by chiral Anderson models. In particular, we study 3-D chiral-orthogonal systems with logarithmic off-diagonal disorder where negative-power ``spikes'' have been observed [2]. We find that at finite disorder strength $W$ of moderate strength, these models in fact do not have a power-singular density of states (DOS) at zero energy in the thermodynamic limit. Rather, this power $p_1$ vanishes and the spectrum features a very accurate power behavior with $p<0$ on an interval around $E = 1$ spreading increasingly closer to $E=0$ and $E = \infty$ with increasing $W$. We connect this to the fact that random hoppings $t$ in these quantum systems are drawn from a scale-invariant $1/t$ distribution regularized via $t \in [e^{-W/2}, e^{W/2}]$, and DOS with negative power can naturally arise inside that range. We show that $\lim_{W \to \infty} p(W, E)=-1$ for all energies accessible by our data. This indicates that, upon removing the cutoff $W$, quantum mechanics transforms the scale-invariant $1/t$ noise into a scale-invariant $1/E$ distribution of eigenstates, which mimics the interpretation of scale-invariant Dirac spectral densities in the IR phase as being due to scale-invariant glue backgrounds [1]. Our results imply that, to model the IR sector of the IR phase, the IR cutoff in chiral Anderson systems needs to be viewed as descending from the randomness strength $W$ rather than the lattice size $L$.

papers.title: Escaping cells dilute CRISPR screen responses unequally across cell types
papers.summary: Single-cell CRISPR screens run in many cell types are used to compare how cell types respond to perturbation, to train models that transfer effects between them and to score such models. These uses assume that cells carrying a guide RNA had their target knocked down. Yet cells grow for days before sequencing: when an essential gene is knocked down, knocked-down cells are depleted or stop dividing while cells that escaped knockdown keep growing, and the measured response, an average over all cells carrying the guide, is diluted. We define the escape fraction of a perturbation as the share of its measured cells whose target was not effectively knocked down, and estimate it from each cell's counts of the targeted gene with a two-group mixture that recovers known fractions in simulated mixtures. In most cell types the escape fraction rises with how essential the gene is, it is higher in a later screen of the same cells, and it reaches about half of the measured cells in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). It predicts how much each response is diluted: the response size falls to (1 - e)^2 of that of the knocked-down cells. Because the escape fraction differs between cell types, it changes all three uses: hESCs respond like K562 cells unless knockdown depletes them, the coefficient a simple transfer model learns is lowered by the dilution of the cell type it predicts, and a benchmark scored on all cells rewards predictions shrunk towards no change, partly because that ground truth is itself diluted. Where cells stop dividing instead, the response also contains expression differences between cell-cycle stages. Response sizes should be compared on knocked-down cells or corrected for the escape fraction.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary Information and data files are included as ancillary files. Code: https://github.com/xuanruihuang/which-cells-are-measured

papers.title: Nuclear fission: from fundamentals to frontiers
papers.summary: Nuclear fission, the division of a heavy atomic nucleus into lighter fragments, is a process of fundamental importance to nuclear physics, energy production, and the origin of the elements. This chapter, part of the Encyclopedia of Nuclear Physics, provides a pedagogical introduction to a broad array of topics in fission physics, progressing from the macroscopic liquid-drop model and microscopic shell corrections through fission dynamics, observables, modern theoretical frameworks, and experimental techniques ranging from traditional double-energy methods to inverse kinematics at radioactive-ion-beam facilities. The roles of fission in astrophysical nucleosynthesis, nuclear energy, medical isotope production, and national security are discussed, and open questions including the predictive power of microscopic theory and the fission properties of neutron-rich nuclei relevant to heavy element nucleosynthesis are highlighted.
papers.comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, for Encyclopedia of Nuclear Physics

papers.title: Kaonic Atom Measurements with the SIDDHARTA-2 Experiment at the DA$Φ$NE accelerator
papers.summary: Kaonic atoms provide a unique experimental tool to investigate low-energy strong interactions in systems containing strangeness and, through high-lying transitions, to test bound-state quantum electrodynamics. The SIDDHARTA-2 experiment at the DA$Φ$NE electron--positron collider performs high-precision X-ray spectroscopy of kaonic atoms using low-momentum charged kaons produced in $φ$-meson decays. Its primary goal is the study of kaonic deuterium through the measurement of X-ray transitions to the ground state, providing direct access to the low-energy $K^-d$ interaction. In parallel, SIDDHARTA-2 has carried out a broad experimental programme with gaseous targets, including kaonic helium-4 and kaonic neon, as well as measurements of high-$n$ transitions in intermediate-mass kaonic atoms formed in the materials of the experimental setup. In this paper, the main SIDDHARTA-2 measurements and their physics motivations are reviewed, together with the experimental strategy developed for kaonic deuterium and the future perspectives of the collaboration within the EXKALIBUR programme.

papers.title: Jet-like dihadron correlations in OO and Ne--Ne collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.36$ TeV with ALICE
papers.summary: Heavy-ion collisions are primarily studied to investigate the properties of hot and dense primordial nuclear matter, known as the quark--gluon plasma (QGP). However, recent observations of hydrodynamic flow--like behavior in pp and p--Pb collisions at the LHC suggest the possible formation of QGP droplets even in the smallest collision systems. To bridge the multiplicity gap between small and large systems and to examine the applicability of hydrodynamic descriptions, light-ion collisions have been studied for the first time at the LHC. This contribution presents dihadron correlation measurements in OO and Ne--Ne collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.36$ TeV recorded with ALICE to explore possible medium effects. The width of the near-side correlation peak has been studied as a function of charged-particle multiplicity at midrapidity, showing a multiplicity-dependent modification of the widths in various transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) intervals in OO and Ne--Ne collisions relative to pp and pO collisions. Further, the per-trigger normalized relative yields of near-side and away-side correlations, $I_{\rm AA}$, are measured in OO collisions for the first time, while in Ne--Ne collisions, the measurement is performed for the near side only. The observed suppression of the away-side associated yield in OO collisions relative to pp collisions is qualitatively consistent with jet--medium interactions, albeit with a weaker magnitude than in central Pb--Pb. However, the extent to which other effects, such as event-selection biases and cold-nuclear-matter effects, contribute to the observed suppression in the present kinematic regime remains an open question.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 2 captioned figures, proceedings of 13th International Conference on Hard and Electromagnetic Probes of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (HP 2026) conference, 21-26 June 2026, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, Tennessee, USA

papers.title: A Barnett-Like Effect in Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collisions
papers.summary: The Barnett effect refers to the spontaneous magnetization or polarization of rotating matter via spin-orbit coupling, a fundamental phenomenon observed across a multitude of physical systems down to atomic scales. Here, we demonstrate that this effect extends to subatomic regimes within relativistic heavy-ion collisions, where the most vortical fluid ever created in terrestrial laboratories is produced and the orbital angular momentum is transferred to emitted hadrons via spin-vorticity coupling. By performing transport simulations spanning a broad energy range, we discover a nearly-linear scaling relation between the global spin polarization of $Λ$ hyperons and the source tilt angle extracted via two-pion femtoscopic correlations. This scaling reveals that global $Λ$ polarization induced by the local vorticity field is modulated by the inclined geometry of the produced strongly-interacting nuclear matter in these collisions. Supported by existing experimental measurements, our results unravel a geometry-modulated Barnett-like effect at the femtometre ($10^{-15}$ m) scale.

papers.title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
papers.summary: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.
papers.comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Dataset and accompanying resources available on Hugging Face under the HelmholtzAI-FZJ organization

papers.title: Comparing Measurements of Pictorial Depth: Conditions for Placing Methods, Observers and Depiction Styles on One Scale
papers.summary: Two observers can agree about what lies in front in a picture yet report different amounts of apparent depth. People report pictorial depth by judging which of two points looks nearer, setting a probe to match a surface, adjusting relative sizes, or rating three-dimensionality. Two such methods can agree closely without sharing a unit. We ask when different methods, observers, depiction styles and viewing conditions can share one scale. Each set of scores, a measurement block, is a graph node. Two blocks are linked only if their shared observations pass six checks fixed in advance, among them outcome type, removal of declared offsets and position effects, proportionality and covariance. If the adjusted shared patterns are exactly proportional, a connected graph fixes every block's gain, its relative scale factor. The checks accept proportionality only within a set margin, so a link supports the gains without proving exact proportionality. One unit is still not one depth coordinate. Suppose each block scores shared stimuli with its own origin and positive unit. A matrix-rank test then decides when a common coordinate is identified: when only one overall origin and unit remain free. If each shared stimulus, an anchor, is scored by exactly two blocks, this needs two disjoint sets of anchors, each connecting every block, their compatibility assumed, not tested. They also suffice, except for anchor values satisfying exact polynomial relations (probability zero for anchor values drawn from any distribution with a density). We adapt network gain estimation from test linking, with a loop-consistency check. A reanalysis of published probe settings on 3-D renderings passes one of 171 candidate depiction-style links through all six checks, each judged by its own 95% bound, unadjusted for the 171 pairs. Links between tasks remain untested; they need shared stimuli and a joint uncertainty model.
papers.comment: 32 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Ancillary files: reproduction package (anc/run_all.sh) with the graph enumeration, exact rank checks, simulations and seeds, and fetch and analysis scripts for the reanalysed public dataset

papers.title: The mathematical journey of spatial reciprocity
papers.summary: Over the past three decades, evolutionary game theory in structured populations has witnessed explosive progress. Counterintuitive cooperative phenomena discovered in simulations have stimulated the development of rigorous mathematical theories to describe the underlying dynamics. In this paper, we review these theoretical advancements, including pair approximation and coalescent theory, which offer analytical solutions to evolutionary games on networks. We summarize the key results obtained by these theories, while also discussing their limitations, such as high computational complexity and constrained flexibility when applied to complex models. We therefore suggest that mathematical approaches provide a complementary tool for understanding cooperation in structured populations alongside simulations.
